newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HSBC Asset Management launches India fund.
newsitem.headline: HSBC Asset Management launches India fund.

text.p: HSBC Asset Management said on Wednesday it has launched a new fund for India, a "country of exceptional promise," according to managing director Christopher Ryan.

In anticipation of improved economic growth forecasts, strong corporate profits and a rebound in stocks, HSBC Asset Management has set up a fund of up to 100 Indian issues listed on the Bombay, Delhi, Calcutta, Ahmedabad, Madras and the National stock exchanges.

"India is not only one of the most attractive markets in Asia, it's one of the most attractive markets in the whole of the emerging market universe," said Carolyn Schloss, director of global emerging markets.
The minimum investment is US$1,000 with inital fees of 5.25 percent and an annual management fee of 1.5 percent.
HSBC is very bullish on India's economic outlook, largely because it projects continued annual exports growth of 11.5 percent for five years.
"Exports have been one of the main engines of India's economic growth and this trend is set to continue," Sanjiv Duggal, HSBC Asset Management's indian equity specialist, said.

Economic growth rates are expected to reach at least 6.5 percent over the next two years, he said. At the same time, the budget deficit is narrowing, real interest rates are falling and liquidity is increasing.
Foreign direct investment is also rising, with HSBC expecting total FDI of US$15 billion by the year 2000 compared to a government forecast of US$10 billion.
Schloss said the fund's investment strategy will be both top-down and bottom-up, and guided by four key themes.

First, infrastructure projects will boost basic industries, telephone companies and power equipment; second, India's vast educated, skilled and cheap workforce will support software and leisure companies; third, rising gross domestic product per capita will help consumer products companies; finally, India's export growth will be led by pharmaceutical and software companies.
